title: India Economic Calendar
description: Scheduled releases of key Indian economic data and RBI events, with previous and actual values.
rows: Manufacturing PMI has now fallen for four consecutive months, from 55.0 in May to 52.8 in August, and while it remains above 50, the unbroken downward trend is more telling than the level itself. Four months of continuous decline is no longer a soft patch. It is a confirmed slowdown, and the gap between where manufacturing was just three months ago and where it is today reflects a demand environment that is deteriorating steadily, not stabilising.

Services PMI recovering from 53.3 to 54.1 is an encouraging reversal after July's sharp drop, suggesting that the domestic demand weakness seen last month was an overcorrection rather than a structural break. However, at 54.1 the sector is still well below where it was earlier this year, and one month of recovery after a steep fall is a stabilisation signal, not a confirmation that the services growth story has resumed.

Reserves jumping from $692.9B to $740.8B in a single month is a sharp turnaround from the months of steady decline, and suggests that foreign money is coming back into India in a meaningful way. This gives the RBI more breathing room than it has had all year, and brings the possibility of an interest rate cut back into the picture if inflation continues to behave.

Food inflation rising to 6% means the cost of groceries and essentials is rising at its fastest pace this year, and it is the main reason headline inflation keeps climbing each month. When food gets more expensive this quickly, it reduces what households have left to spend on everything else, which puts pressure on the very domestic consumption that has been holding up India's economy.

Government capex swinging from 53.7% growth to a 29.9% contraction in a single month means the one engine that has been keeping India's growth story intact has stalled sharply. With manufacturing slowing for four straight months, services still recovering, and inflation keeping the RBI on hold, a sudden pullback in government spending removes the last active support the economy had going into Q3 FY27.

A jump of 2.3 points in a single month, after four consecutive months of decline, is a strong reversal and suggests that the manufacturing slowdown was shallower than the trend implied. However, one month of recovery after a prolonged slide is a reason for cautious optimism, not a confirmation that the sector has turned a corner. The next reading will matter more than this one.

Services PMI rising to 55.2 marks the second consecutive month of improvement, suggesting the sharp July drop was a temporary dip rather than the start of a deeper slowdown. With both manufacturing and services now moving up together for the first time in months, the growth picture is looking more balanced than it has at any point since May, which is a meaningful shift in the overall economic direction.

The RBI raised rates by 25 basis points, the first hike after a long pause, confirming that persistently rising inflation has forced the central bank's hand despite signs of economic recovery in both PMIs. A rate hike at a time when manufacturing and services are just beginning to recover tells us the RBI has decided that controlling inflation is more urgent than protecting growth, which changes the outlook for borrowing costs and interest-sensitive sectors for the rest of FY27.

Reserves rising for the second consecutive month to $747.6B confirms that the sharp drawdown seen earlier this year has genuinely reversed, and foreign capital is flowing back into India with consistency. Two months of consecutive reserve buildup alongside a rate hike signals that the RBI is now operating from a position of strength rather than pressure, which is a fundamentally different and more stable environment than what existed just three months ago.
